complexity_matrix.notes: Cost is the tree height H, not the node count. H = O(log N) when balanced, O(N) when degenerate.
Same descent as search plus one pointer assignment, so the bound is the height H. Degenerates identically to search.

complexity_matrix.operation: Delete a node with 0 or 1 child
complexity_matrix.notes: Given the node pointer, the splice itself is O(1); locating it costs the height H.
Descends to the in-order successor and splices it out; a constant number of descents, each O(H).

complexity_matrix.operation: Lower bound on height for any binary tree
complexity_matrix.notes: A height-H binary tree holds at most 2^(H+1) - 1 nodes, so N <= 2^(H+1) - 1 forces H >= log2(N+1) - 1. Structural, not implementation-specific.
Time is Theta(N) because every node must be read. Recursion or an explicit stack holds at most H entries; O(H) is O(N) for a degenerate tree, which can overflow the call stack.
W is the maximum width. For a complete tree W = N/2, so this is O(N) space — the one traversal whose space is not O(H).

complexity_matrix.operation: Report tree height or count leaves only
complexity_matrix.notes: Stops at the shallowest leaf rather than visiting every node, so it beats a full traversal whenever the tree is wide.

complexity_matrix.operation: Range query over keys in [k1, k2]
complexity_matrix.notes: Descend to the first key >= k1, then walk successors while <= k2. R is the number of results and is unavoidable output.
The capability a hash table cannot provide at any price, and the reason ordered structures exist.

complexity_matrix.operation: Membership lookup for comparison against hashing
complexity_matrix.notes: A balanced tree is strictly worse than a hash table for membership alone (O(log N) vs O(1) expected). The tree is justified only by order-dependent operations.

complexity_matrix.operation: Insert sorted keys into an unbalanced BST
complexity_matrix.notes: Each key descends to the rightmost node, producing a linked list of height N-1. Every later operation silently degrades to O(N).
Bounded rotations along the insertion path. This O(log N) per insert is the price paid to keep height at O(log N) and so keep lookups logarithmic.

correctness_argument.claim: The BST invariant makes each comparison discard exactly one subtree, so the search path never leaves the subtree containing the target and reaching a null link proves absence. In two-child deletion, replacing the node's key with its in-order successor's key preserves ordering relative to both subtrees, because the successor is the minimum of the right subtree.

cost_derivations.claim: Search cost equals the height H because each step follows one edge on a root-to-leaf path; since a height-H binary tree holds at most 2^(H+1) - 1 nodes, H is at least log2(N+1) - 1 for every binary tree, so O(log N) is optimal for balanced trees and O(N) for degenerate ones.

limits.claim: O(log N) search is optimal among comparison-based binary trees because the height bound is structural. Order-preserving structures for fixed-width keys reach O(log log U) but pay space proportional to the universe, so the improvement is bought with memory rather than found.
